topic.name: The Inner Product in Vector Spaces Over the Complex Numbers

question.text:
Given that $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $\mathbb{C},$ find $\big\langle \mathbf{a}, \: 6\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c} \big\rangle$ if

$\qquad$ $ \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 2+3\text{i} \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = 3+8\text{i}.$
question.explanation:
Recall that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ satisfies the following properties.

  • It is linear in the first argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \alpha \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It has conjugate symmetry. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}.$

  • It is positive-definite. For any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ is a non-negative real number, and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $\mathbb{C} $ is antilinear in the second argument:

\begin{align*} \big\langle \mathbf{a}, \: 6\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c} \big\rangle &= \langle \mathbf{a}, 6\mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \\[5pt] &= \overline{6} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle\\[5pt] &= 6 \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \end{align*}

Next, we use the fact that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ has conjugate symmetry:

\begin{align*} 6 \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle &= 6 \overline{ \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle } + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, we substitute the values for $\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 6 \overline{ \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle } + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle &= 6 (\overline{2+3\text{i} }) + (3+8\text{i}) \\[5pt] &= 6 (2-3\text{i}) + (3+8\text{i}) \\[5pt] &= 12 -18\text{i} +3 +8\text{i} \\[5pt] &= 15 -10\text{i} \end{align*}

example.title: Applying Properties of the Hermitian Inner Product

question.text:
Given that $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $\mathbb{C},$ find $\big\langle \mathbf{a}, \: \mathbf{b}+(2+5\text{i})\mathbf{c} \big\rangle$ if

$\qquad$ $ \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 3-\text{i} \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle =\text{i} .$
question.explanation:
Recall that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ satisfies the following properties.

  • It is linear in the first argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \alpha \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It has conjugate symmetry. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}.$

  • It is positive-definite. For any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ is a non-negative real number, and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ is antilinear in the second argument:

\begin{align*} \big\langle \mathbf{a}, \: \mathbf{b}+(2+5\text{i})\mathbf{c} \big\rangle &= \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, (2+5\text{i})\mathbf{c} \rangle \\[5pt] &= \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + (\overline{2+5\text{i}}) \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \\[5pt] &= \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + (2-5\text{i}) \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \end{align*}

Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ has conjugate symmetry:

\begin{align*} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + (2-5\text{i}) \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle &= \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle} + (2-5\text{i}) \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, we substitute the values for $\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle} + (2-5\text{i}) \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle &= \overline{3-\text{i}} + (2-5\text{i}) \cdot \text{i} \\[5pt] &= 3 + \text{i} + (2-5\text{i}) \cdot \text{i} \\[5pt] &= 3 + \text{i} +2 \text{i} - 5(-1)\\[5pt] &= 8 + 3\text{i} \end{align*}

example.title: Applying Properties of the Hermitian Inner Product

question.text:
Given that $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $\mathbb{C},$ find $\big\langle \mathbf{a}, \: (4-\text{i})\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c} \big\rangle$ if

$\qquad$ $ \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = -1-\text{i} \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = 5.$
question.explanation:
Recall that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ satisfies the following properties.

  • It is linear in the first argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \alpha \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It has conjugate symmetry. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}.$

  • It is positive-definite. For any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ is a non-negative real number, and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ is antilinear in the second argument:

\begin{align*} \big\langle \mathbf{a}, \: (4-\text{i})\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c} \big\rangle &= \langle \mathbf{a}, (4-\text{i})\mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \\[5pt] &= (\overline{4-\text{i}}) \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle +\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \\[5pt] &= (4+\text{i}) \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle +\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \end{align*}

Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ has conjugate symmetry:

\begin{align*} (4+\text{i}) \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle +\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \ \rangle &= (4+\text{i}) \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle} + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, we substitute the values for $\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} (4+\text{i}) \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle} + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c}\rangle &= (4+\text{i})\cdot (\overline{-1-\text{i}}) + 5 \\[5pt] &= (4+\text{i})\cdot ({-1+\text{i}}) + 5 \\[5pt] &= - 5+3\text{i} +5 \\[5pt] &= 3\text{i} \end{align*}

example.title: Applying Properties of the Hermitian Inner Product

question.text:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ over $\mathbb{C}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = {\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}$ for any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n$
  2. $\langle\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a},\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ for any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n$
  3. $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle\in\mathbb R$ for any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n$
question.explanation:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ satisfies the following properties:

  • It is linear in the first argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \alpha \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It has conjugate symmetry. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}.$

  • It is positive-definite. For any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ is a non-negative real number, and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. The inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ has conjugate symmetry.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, by the linearity in the first argument and the antilinearity in the second argument we have \[\langle\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a},\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a} \rangle =(\mathrm{i}\cdot \bar{ \mathrm{i} })\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = -\mathrm{i}^2\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle= \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle. \]

  • Statement III is false. The inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ is a complex number, in general.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

example.title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product

question.text:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ over $\mathbb{C}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = {\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}$ for any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n$
  2. $\langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle$ for any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle> {0}$ for any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n$
question.explanation:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ satisfies the following properties:

  • It is linear in the first argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \alpha \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

  • It has conjugate symmetry. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}.$

  • It is positive-definite. For any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

    $\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ is a non-negative real number, and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. The inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ has conjugate symmetry.

  • Statement II is true. For any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R},$ we have $\overline{\alpha} = \alpha.$ Therefore, \[\langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.\]

  • Statement III is false. Notice that if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0},$ then $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
